Crash Course Philosophy is brought to you
by Squarespace. Squarespace: share your passion with the world. Who is The Doctor? Is it this guy?
Or this one? How about him? As any good Whovian knows, the answer is yes,
all of them. But, also, wait: No. In the show Doctor Who, each incarnation of
The Doctor has a completely different body, different mannerisms, likes and dislikes and,
to some extent, memories. So… how are they all The Doctor? Science fiction is great at giving us scenarios to grapple with that seem far-out and only barely possible. But when you think about it, the issue of Who is Who isn’t that much more clear-cut in real life. The fact is, you can take the same questions I asked about The Doctor, and ask them about anyone. Like…me. I mean, are these people any more similar
to each other…than these people? [Theme Music] Last time, we talked about identity – or basically, what makes an object the same over time. And the concept can get more complex when we talk about our own identity, or the identity of others. When talking about ships or trees, we might be willing to say yeah, ok, that’s just not the same thing it used to be. But when we’re talking about, say, me! I have the strong belief that I’m the same person that mom and dad brought home from the hospital back in 1980. I’m that same kid that cut his hand open
on that broken flower pot – I have the scar to prove it! And there’s some guy in the future who’s still going to be me, even though he’ll be all stooped over, and wrinkled, and gray.
At least, I hope. And you probably think of yourself in the same way – that you’ll keep being the same person, from birth to death. But, you could argue
– and some have – that the only thing that really remains constant
about you your whole life is your name. And for some of us, even that changes! Philosophers have struggled with the issue
of personal identity for a long time, trying to find that special something – that
essential property – that makes you you, the thing that preserves
your identity through time, and through all the changes that come with
it. Let’s take a look at some of ideas they’ve
come up with. First there’s the Body Theory. This is sort of the default position that
most people have – and the assumption that Doctor Who messes
with so badly. It says that personal identity persists over time because you remain in the same body from birth to death. Now, in a sense, that’s true – I don’t know anybody outside of, like, Freaky Friday that’s had a body transplant. But, it’s not like you consist of all of the same, identical stuff that you had when you were born. You’ve sloughed off and replaced your outer
layer of skin, for example, hundreds of times so far. Your red blood cells only live about 4 months
before they’re cycled out. Even your skeleton is constantly being remodeled. So, kind of like the Doctor – or the Ship
of Theseus – you’re constantly being replaced by new
physical versions of yourself. And if you are your body, then how much of
you can change until you become a new you? Can you get a haircut? What if you lose or
gain a lot of weight? Or grow a beard? Or put John Travolta’s
face on your face? Let’s go over to the Thought Bubble and explore the ideas of our bodies, and ourselves, with some Flash Philosophy! 20th century English moral philosopher Bernard
Williams proposed a thought experiment, to make us consider where we think our personal
identity resides. It goes something like this:
You and I have been kidnapped by a mad scientist. He tells us that, tomorrow morning, he’s
going to transfer all of your mental content – all of your beliefs, memories, personality,
everything – into my brain. And then he’s gonna move all of my mental
content into your brain. Presumably, this is how he earned the title
of mad scientist. But he also tells us that, after the procedure
is complete – and your mental content is in this body,
and my mental content is in yours – he’ll give one of the bodies a million dollars,
and the other body will be tortured. And he’s decided to let you pick which body
gets the torture and which one gets the cash. What do you decide? Your answer should give you a clue about where you think your identity lies. Thanks, Thought Bubble! Now our friend John Locke didn’t cotton to the idea that the most essential aspect of a person is her body. For Locke, the thing that makes you you is
the non-physical stuff – your consciousness. But Locke recognized that we don’t maintain a single consciousness over the course of our entire lives. We go to sleep every day, but, when we wake up, our conscious selves remember who we were the day before. So Locke posited a Memory Theory of personal
identity. He believed that your identity persists over time, because you retain memories of yourself at different points, and each of those memories is connected to
one before it. Now, we don’t remember every single moment – I mean, do you remember what you ate for lunch last Tuesday? But you can probably remember a time when you did remember that – like, say, last Tuesday afternoon. And if you can remember that version of yourself, then you’re still connected to the Tuesday-at-lunch
person, through a chain of memory. And this process can take us back a lot farther
than last Tuesday. Locke said that if you can remember back to
your first day of kindergarten, you maintain a memory link to that person. Sure, your Mom also remembers that day, but
no one remembers it from the inside – the butterflies in your stomach; the way your new shoes felt stiff after a summer of running barefoot. That’s your memory, and since it’s yours, you must be the same person who experienced that memory.

Crash Course Philosophy Summary

Part 1: The Doctor's Dilemma

The "Doctor Who" television series presents an intriguing paradox: each incarnation of The Doctor (and this idea applies to humanity) has a completely unique body, demeanor, preferences, and memories. So is there only one true version of the character? This question explores whether identity can be definitively connected to a specific individual through personal history or external experiences. The concept of identity is explored in philosophical terms: if all parts of your body change over time - skin, blood cells, even bones - are those changes simply transformations or alterations that fundamentally alter who you were? The "Doctor Who" analogy offers a visual representation of self-change throughout life.

Part 2: Body and Thought as Identity

While the common assumption is that physical consistency remains consistent over time (body is fixed). the philosopher Bernard Williams proposed an experiment to highlight this. He posed what would likely lead to a "mad scientist" dilemma. A mental transfer process where all personality traits are relocated from one individual into another's body, leading to two distinct individuals. This scenario raises questions about the core of personal identity if bodily consistency changes over time * **Body Theory:** In this popular view, the person's identity is inherently linked to their physical form and changes over life events happen in a new physical space (like skin replacement). * **Flash Philosophy & Thought Bubble Exploration:** The theory challenges how long a core part of someone's individual nature can be retained when bodily changes occur.

Part 3: Locke and Memory Theory

John Locke, who favored consciousness rather than body as the origin of identity. He argued that personal memory serves as concrete evidence to support consistency, even if you can't always remember specific moments or days. The passage argues this with the assumption we all retain a long-lasting memory connected to our personal history: * **Locke's Memory Theory:** Locke believed identity persisted based on past experiences (specifically our memories) and how we maintain connections to prior versions of ourselves throughout time . * **Locke's Argument:** With the help of a childhood example, he proposed that if a person remembers a particular moment or memory related to a specific day from their early life. For Locke, this memory could indicate that they remain the same person in essence – even as their physical body changes over time.

### The Nature of Personal Identity: 
A Discussion of Theories

This transcript examines various theories regarding personal identity.  It explores what aspects of a person remain constant over time, especially across a lifespan. 


**The Body Theory:** This theory states that personal identity persists because the physical body remains consistent throughout life. While the notion is intuitive, it's challenged by the constant transformation of our bodies through skin changes, blood cell cycles, and bone remodeling. Over time, individuals undergo substantial physical modifications, such as shedding old skin layers or undergoing changes in size and appearance. This suggests that our bodily self  replaces itself, challenging the very nature of "same person." 

**The Thought Bubble Theory:** As a thought experiment, this theory explores where true personal identity resides. In this hypothetical scenario, a  mad scientist transfers one's memories to another body.  Then the decision as to who will receive the cash and who suffers from torture is left in your hands: How do you decide? This thought experiment suggests that if we truly understand our core selves are made up of the most fundamental elements of our consciousness and experiences, it may help us define personal identity. 

**The Memory Theory:**  Philosopher John Locke proposed this theory.  Locke asserted that consciousness, rather than the body, defines personal identity. He believed memories link us across time as "We retain memories of ourselves at different points, and each of those memories is shaped by the one before it." This framework suggests that your individual story is built through a chain of moments, connecting you to previous versions of yourself.


**Challenges to the Memory Theory:**
Despite its allure, this theory runs into obstacles due to limitations in human consciousness: 
* **The Inherent Flaw to Birth Memory:** Due to the nature of our birth experience (or lack thereof), no one can ever recall those very early life stages with clarity or complete accuracy. This may imply that someone's identity is not yet solidified. 

* **Loss of Memories and Identity Shifts:** Memory theory creates uncertainty due to the possibility of amnesia or memory loss during later years. When individuals succumb to dementia, they face a significant challenge - losing their capacity for recalling past events, impacting their sense of self and how we perceive the nature of identity itself.


**The Complexity of False Memories: ** The human mind, through the lens of memories, can create narratives or experiences that may not be accurate.  This creates challenges in understanding memory's reliability because it doesn’t always reflect reality accurately.

**Conclusion:** As argued by Locke and explored across numerous theories on identity, a defining core to how we are is through our shared experiences across time. The questions of false memories and their impact remain a complex topic of research as we attempt to understand how deeply entrenched these experiences are in who we become.

Exploring Personal Identity

**Introduction & Background** The concept of personal identity involves understanding how individuals persist through time. This discussion explores different theories of personal identity, ranging from body theory to thought-bubble philosophies. **Body Theory** * The body theory posits that personal identity persists over time due to our physical bodies remaining relatively unchanged until death. * Challenges to this view arise from observing continuous physical change, such as skin cell renewal or bone remodeling. This suggests the body’s constant changes are fundamental to identity, challenging a purely body-centric view of who we are at the end. **Thought-bubble Philosophies** Philosophers like Bernard Williams and John Locke offer thought experiments that delve into the nature of personal identity. * **Williams' Thought Experiment:** The experiment presents a hypothetical situation where someone’s mental content (personality, beliefs) is transferred between two bodies. * This would prompt an existential evaluation by the person who experiences this change – revealing something about their own identity in this specific space. **Locke's Memory Theory** * Locke argued that personal identity lies in consciousness, not physical body-features alone. * Locke emphasized the importance of memories that link different moments in time and contribute to our sense of self. * By tracing his mental path through time based on distinct memories, he argues that a person's connection is established. **Challenges to Locke's theory:** Memory theory faces problems with the loss of memory and how we recall events accurately. Furthermore, it raises questions about personal identity during birth and life’s end— when significant alterations may occur. * The very act of remembering one’s own development challenges traditional notions since some memories are hard to recall. **Memory's Difficulty & False Memories** Memory’s reliability is debated with many false memories cropping up in human experiences and eyewitness accounts. Can we truly trust the memories of events that occurred in the past? It has significant impacts for personal identity, as accuracy may be subjective rather than objective. ** The Significance of Personal Identity** * Real-world application: How personal identity plays out in our day-to-day lives and responsibilities is critical. * Obligations like work/salary promises or relationships often assume that individuals are constant over time – impacting all aspects of life. The question remains—how much weight does personal identity hold and how we measure it? It has profound implications for our understanding of oneself, one's behavior and responsibilities.

The Body Theory proposes that personal identity persists due to staying in the same body from birth to death. However, this is not entirely true; as our skin sheds hundreds of times and cells, such as red blood cells, only last four months before being cycled out. Even bones are continuously remodeling. Therefore, one's "being" is constantly changing, resembling the Doctor or Ship of Theseus idea. If "body" represents a person's identity, at what point does change constitute a new "self"? Can a haircut or weight changes denote a transformation?  Let's explore the thoughts surrounding identity, as proposed by philosophers. 
English moral philosopher Bernard Williams developed a thought experiment to help us understand identity. Imagine you and I are kidnapped by a mad scientist who will transfer our minds into each other the next day. This is his mad-science approach. The "identity transfer," resulting in one body receiving wealth and the other, torture. He chooses whether which entity's body receives what. What do you choose? Your answer reveals your perception of where we find our personal identities. Thank you for participating in Thought Bubble! 
John Locke disagreed with the idea that a person's entire essence resides in their physique.  Locke believed the non-physical stuff – consciousness - was crucial to defining who a person is. He acknowledged, though, that identity maintains over time via memories and past experiences. We retain memories of ourselves throughout diverse stages. This process, which can reach back even longer than one Tuesday afternoon; Locke's "Memory Theory" makes sense but also presents challenges:  First, no one remembers their birth. The truth is, none would enjoy remembering their earliest years – poop diapers or not – and we all had those first few early years that were, indeed, a significant part of our formative experiences. If identity necessitates memory, individuals must start gaining identities even when they are younger and then the beginning needs to be covered. As such, we lack complete personal history and may struggle with this theory as a matter of practical effect on "real-life" experience if people lose memories - their identity changes with time: It's hard to say whether someone losing their memory impacts who they truly are; or if it truly makes the difference.  

Lastly, Locke’s theory also presents challenges for our understanding and experiences – memory is fragile as well. What's more challenging, since we know that a group of eyewitnesses will often recount events quite differently despite similar settings. The extent to which memories are accurate is not always clear. A common question that arises - How can we confirm whether faulty memories alter their identity or how such distorted recollections impact them? To this end, our lives have been shaped by the idea that individuals remain the same, unchanged and consistent throughout our living existence; but what if it's not so simple as "identity" itself might need re-examining and reevaluating?

Finally, for a greater understanding of identity
and how to live with authenticity: When considering obligations towards people in life – what does this mean for those who we have to depend upon. If people are not the same, they may be less obligated or may not have these bonds. How others think of us is dependent on our identity staying constant over time; if that is now a shifting landscape, their perceptions of the "self" could also change. We must consider how to navigate identity as humans become more and more complex over time in a nuanced way. It's a significant question to ponder: Is this really worth considering or are these simply a matter of abstract philosophy and self-experimentation?

###  Personal Identity: The Internal Compass & the Debate

This video explores the fundamental question of personal identity. Two main theories attempt to answer this question, each with its own set of problems.

**The Mad Scientist Experiment**
The video begins with a thought experiment where a mad scientist hypothetically transfers someone's mental content to another person's body, and vice versa. Following this transfer, the mad scientist then decides which body will receive financial reward (i.e., money) and torture. It's hoped that observing the impact on one body might shed light on the nature of selfhood as our bodies are different from each other at least in terms of where the mental content is located.

**John Locke's Theory: Consciousness as Identity Key**
John Locke argued that what defines a person goes beyond the physical. He posited that a person's identity arises from the persistency of their consciousness over time, connected through memories. This memory trail serves to represent how we remain the same person across our lives; for example, if one can recall Tuesday afternoon from 7 years ago, they are still linked to the Tuesday-at-lunch person.

**Memory Theory: Uncovering Its Challenges**
 The memory theory presents a valid argument by suggesting that consciousness and memory persist through physical changes. But, it also encounters significant challenges—namely the human instinct to forget key moments, like birth or early childhood experiences. If we follow Locke's theory for our entire life, this poses questions for identity as our memories are fluid; they change and shift throughout time. 

 **The Problem of False Memories**
Furthermore, the problem of false memories and the lack of certainty in memory reliability highlight the complexity of personal identity. It highlights the challenge between what one remembers having or doing versus truth, which is important when trying to build an understanding of personal identity, and can further hinder our ability to create a reliable self from within.  

 **The Importance of Personhood & Consequences**
Does the persistence of self through physical changes provide true answers on personality? The video argues no because it relies solely on memory and may not give complete answers for identity formation. It also presents questions about who we are in our personal relationships, obligations and responsibilities based on our belief in this concept.


 **Moving Forward: The Value of Personhood**
The concluding sections discuss the broader implications of personhood and examine how it impacts daily life, such as expectations in employment, relationships and societal engagements. Overall, understanding self-identity is crucial for navigating our lives and building authentic personhood through a constant challenge. 


###  Conclusion and Outro

For a clearer look at this phenomenon, please remember to watch the next episode on personal identity! Don't forget to subscribe if you'd like to further discuss these concepts. The video concludes by thanking Squarespace for its support in making this content available.

He believed that your identity persists over time because you retain memories of yourself at different points, each of those memories is connected to one before it.  

Now, we don’t remember every single moment - I mean, do you remember what you ate for lunch last Tuesday? But you can probably remember a time when you did – like, say, last Tuesday afternoon. And if you can remember that version of yourself, then you’re still connected to the Tuesday-at-lunch person, through a chain of memory.  And this process can take us back a lot farther than last Tuesday. Locke said that if you can remember back to your first day of kindergarten, you maintain a memory link to that person. Sure, your mom also remembers that day, but no one remembers it from the inside - the butterflies in your stomach; the way your new shoes felt stiff after a summer of running barefoot. That’s your memory, and since it's yours, you must be the same person who experienced that memory.  The memory theory actually makes a lot of sense, but it has some problems of its own. 

First off, no one remembers being born. Now that’s not a bad thing at all - I mean, think about what life would be without learning to exist from scratch. Maybe all you feel like you need to know is that your self has to go to work and pay bills, and that's plenty.

But the matter of personal identity isn’t just a conceptual puzzle. It's also deeply important when you’re thinking about how you should live your life. For example  do you believe you have obligations to particular people in your life? Well, if those people don't persist as distinct identities, then your obligations might not either. And the same goes for how people think about you. Your boss only has to give you the raise she promised you, if each of you remains the same person you were when she made the promise.  In fact, if next Friday, you’re not the same person anymore, doesn't even have to pay you!  The fact is, we’ve all built our lives and our society on the expectations that individuals will continue to be who they are, unchanged — and those people expect the same thing out of you. So now you can see… this really is your problem. You expect a paycheck. You expect people to keep their promises.  But as we learned back with Clifford and James and epistemic responsibility, you don’t just get to believe things without reasons. So if you think you deserve that paycheck, you need to figure out why. 

 Today we talked about personal identity. We considered the two main answers people give to the question of where your identity lies - in your body, or in the connected memories of your consciousness.  We found some significant problems with each of them, and then we talked about why the persistence of identity is actually something you should care about! Next time, we’ll return to this issue and talk about whether you really need the idea of a “you” that persists over time. If you still exist then, I hope you join me.

**Personal Identity: A Summary**

Memories are fundamental to personal identity. John Locke posited a memory theory, suggesting that personal identity persists over time through memories of past selves. The sequence of experiences builds a cohesive identity. However, there are challenges within this theory. 

Firstly, human beings do not possess recollections of being born. This raises questions about how we begin as individuals –  if memories of the day after birth don't exist, does this indicate an absence of self-awareness from that day onward? Furthermore, memory loss can dramatically alter one's identity, especially in cases of dementia impacting people's past experiences. 

Next, memory itself raises significant issues. Memories are often unreliable and even contradictory, challenging the accuracy of our recollections; these inaccuracies may impact the definition of who we are when compared to what our memories reflect. The challenge lies in reconciling accuracy with faulty information to define personal identity.

Locke's theory also faces difficulty aligning with constant change, as memory is not immune to physical changes, such as aging and bodily degradation. Both Locke's "memory" theory and the "body-theory" face significant challenges when examining the nature of personal identity. A lingering question about this discussion of identity concerns false memories - how to distinguish accurate recollections from inaccurate ones? 

**Significance and Implications**

The concept of personal identity profoundly shapes our lives and society:
* **Obligations:** Personal identity forms duty obligations – if identities disappear, so too do the inherent commitments such as work-related promises and familial expectations.  
* **Living:** Our belief in a persistent self impacts how we navigate life - both in terms of future decisions, relationships, and expectations regarding outcomes from our choices.

**Moving Forward**

Will personal identity persist outside traditional frameworks? Next time, the video will delve into the "you" issue and the validity of these conceptions.  This series explores these ideas: memory theory of personal identity, body theory – the debate about what constitutes true self-identity; how accurate recollections may inform who we consider ourselves to be.
